idiom_name: func(T) bool predicate values + a hand-written loop in a container method (slices.*Func, iter.Seq)
implementation_notes: Go has no generic Filter in the standard library and no inheritance, so the criterion is an ordinary function value - type ThreatFilter func(Threat) bool - and filtering is a hand-written loop that appends survivors to a fresh slice; the slices package only ships predicate-taking helpers for search and in-place deletion (ContainsFunc, IndexFunc, DeleteFunc, CompactFunc). The container-typed result is a method on the container that returns a new value with the same id, which is the pattern's 'filtered version of itself' in Go's idiom. Since Go 1.23 the lazy form is expressible with iter.Seq and composed filters (func(iter.Seq[E]) iter.Seq[E]) consumed by slices.Collect/AppendSeq, which is what the standard library's own iterator helpers do; keep the plain loop for a single criterion, since it is shorter and allocation-free beyond the result.
pitfalls: The in-place helpers (slices.DeleteFunc) mutate and return the same backing array, so a 'filtered' slice that shares it changes when the source changes; copy out of the source when the container copies are meant to be independent.
Function values are not comparable, so criteria cannot be deduplicated or used as map keys; named predicate variables are also the only way to document intent.
Each chained filter allocates a slice, and slices.Collect returns nil for an empty sequence, so a chain of filters over a large slice costs more than one composed predicate.
A predicate that mutates the slice being iterated (or that is run concurrently with writers) races: copying the elements first, or filtering a snapshot, is the safe pattern.
